quote: By your company, and you guys keep calling me and texting me.
stewart_read: Customer is flagging that this is a repeat/recycled contact on a lead Ion already disqualified. The rep proceeds with a standard qualify flow instead of recognizing this as a re-contact of a closed record.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may not have access to prior-call notes and is discovering this live, making the continued qualify attempt understandable rather than a procedural failure.
coaching_implication: Check whether reps have visibility into prior-DQ status before dialing recycled leads; if not, this is a systems gap, not purely a rep skill gap — but the rep should still ask directly and early whether this home was already assessed before continuing.

quote: I just I'm a little did they say why it wouldn't work? Because I'm looking on the map, so it looks fine.
stewart_read: Rep transparently admits uncertainty and pulls up a satellite/mapping tool live rather than dismissing the customer's claim outright. This is the 'admit and recover with transparency' pattern, which is the better of the three knowledge-gap responses the schema tracks.
coaching_implication: This is a fine moment of honesty, but it also reveals the rep had zero pre-call context on a lead with a documented DQ history — worth flagging as a prep gap rather than a rep judgment gap.

quote: I mean, I could try to see what we could do. Are you willing to, like, use trimming trees?
stewart_read: Rep never captured a bill number or usage figure before proposing a technical workaround; the offer to trim trees is a specific fix pitched with no anchor to the customer's actual bill pain, so there's nothing pulling her back in emotionally even if trimming were feasible.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be trying to salvage the DQ with a concrete, testable ask (tree trimming) rather than re-litigating the shade claim in the abstract, which is a reasonable troubleshooting instinct given the circumstances.
coaching_implication: Before offering technical workarounds, anchor to what the customer would gain (bill relief) so the workaround has a payoff attached — right now it's a bare procedural ask with no value frame.

quote: there's not enough surface area on the back of the house that doesn't get shade or gets enough sun to take away the power bill. It's not worth it.
stewart_read: This is a technical roof/orientation/shading assessment the customer is delivering, and the correct setter move is to route it to a specialist for an actual site evaluation rather than adjudicate feasibility on a phone call. The rep instead continues to informally assess feasibility live (map look, trimming question) rather than deferring to design/specialist review.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer already has a firm prior DQ from Ion itself, an immediate escalation to a specialist site visit may not have been warranted either — the shade issue may be genuinely settled.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep on using the escape hatch language ('that's exactly what our design team evaluates on site') instead of personally weighing shade/orientation feasibility over the phone, even when trying to be helpful.

quote: Well, I can here. I can help you get a phone call. That way you don't have to sit and meet with anybody and waste your time.
stewart_read: Rep offers a low-friction phone-only appointment as a way to keep the lead alive after the customer has twice rejected the premise, but does not name any day or time — it is a vague reassurance, not a booking attempt.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: the rep may be trying to de-escalate before pushing for a specific time, planning to lock a slot only if the customer responds positively. But the customer's immediate 'No. I'd be wasting my time.' shows the offer did not land and no follow-up attempt to anchor a time was made.
coaching_implication: When offering a fallback appointment type as a save, still anchor a concrete day/time immediately — a vague offer gives the customer nothing concrete to say yes to and reads as filler.

quote: Let me ask my manager if you're willing to because you're willing to trim up if it'll work. Just I'll go find out right now.
stewart_read: Rep places the customer on hold to consult a manager about a scenario (extreme shade requiring tree removal, HOA-restricted placement, prior DQ) that falls outside the standard qualify-and-book script, matching the non-standard-scenario-hold pattern rather than a simple knowledge gap.
coaching_implication: This was the right instinct — escalate an edge case rather than guess — but it happened after several minutes of live technical debate rather than immediately once the prior-DQ was disclosed at 00:17-00:24.

quote: So you were right. We're not allowed to do anything because it is too shaky.
stewart_read: The manager check confirms the home is a hard DQ (excessive shade, no viable placement), which the customer had already told the rep at 00:17-00:24. Four minutes were spent re-verifying a conclusion the customer stated up front.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be required to verify DQs independently rather than take a customer's self-report at face value, which would make the re-check procedurally correct even though it wastes time.
coaching_implication: If self-reported prior DQs can be trusted, empower reps to confirm and close faster; if not, this is a process question for Kenny, not purely a rep-skill gap.

quote: Please please remove me from the list.
stewart_read: The call ends with an explicit do-not-contact request after the customer describes repeated unwanted calls/texts on an already-disqualified home. There is no rep acknowledgment beyond a polite close.
coaching_implication: This suppression request needs to be logged and enforced immediately — repeat contact on a hard-DQ, opt-out lead is a compliance and brand-trust risk, not just a missed-booking call.
